messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 23
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: UX Designer
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 75

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Workplace: Workplace, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims, Victim Similarity: People who look similar to the victims
  Maladaptive Strategies: Prevention Rumination: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle

Vignette:
Aisha Patel was 23 when she sought treatment, a married South Asian American woman working as a UX designer at a mid-sized tech company. The event she returned to again and again had happened on an ordinary weekday evening after work. She had been driving home, tired and preoccupied, replaying comments from a design review in her head while moving through a busy intersection not far from her office. In the seconds that followed, another person was seriously injured. What stayed with Aisha was not only that someone had been hurt, but that she had been involved in causing it. She remembered seeing the other person on the ground and the sickening certainty that her own actions had become part of someone else’s life in the worst possible way. In the immediate aftermath she could think only, This should not have happened. I should have stopped it.

In the weeks that followed, the event attached itself to the places and people around her in ways that made daily life feel dangerous and morally charged. Returning to her workplace was especially difficult because the accident had happened on her commute, in the orbit of her office routine. Walking into the building each morning, seeing the parking garage, or hearing coworkers talk casually about traffic or commuting could make her stomach drop. Even opening the rideshare app to avoid driving herself brought on a rush of images of that evening. At work, when teammates asked if she wanted to join lunch off-site or ride with them to a user interview, she would quickly make excuses. The office had once been a place where she stayed late sketching interfaces and debating details with colleagues; now it was bound up with the memory of leaving work and what happened next.

Certain people also became unexpectedly potent reminders. If she passed someone who looked similar to the injured person, she felt herself go rigid and stare for a second too long, as if checking whether they were the same person or whether some version of the event was about to happen again. She found this deeply unsettling and shameful. In public she tried to lower her gaze, but that only made her more alert to faces, bodies, and movements around her. When something directly reminded her of the victim, she felt pulled back to the scene with a force she could not control. She would later describe these moments less as ordinary remembering than as being overtaken by the fact that someone had been hurt and that she had been there, had done something, had failed to prevent it.

Aisha spent long stretches of time trying to work out exactly how the event could have been prevented. On the train to work, in the shower, lying beside her husband at night, she mentally reconstructed the timing of the light, the position of the car, the speed, her own attention, the possible decision points. If she had left five minutes later. If she had taken a different route. If she had ignored the work comments she was replaying. If she had been more careful, more responsible, more like the kind of person who never lets something like this happen. These thoughts did not arrive as abstract reflection; they came with urgency, as if solving the sequence might still somehow undo what had happened or prove she was not the kind of person who could seriously injure someone.

At the same time, she worked hard not to think about the trauma at all. She threw herself into wireframes and usability flows, filled silence with podcasts, and kept multiple tabs open so there was always something to look at. When an image or memory broke through, she would clamp down on it immediately, straighten in her chair, and force herself back to the screen. Colleagues noticed she was quieter in meetings and less willing to stay for informal chats. Her husband began doing nearly all of the driving. If they needed groceries, he went alone or they ordered delivery. If family invited them somewhere across town, Aisha would say she was tired or had work to finish rather than admit that even being a passenger made her body tense and her mind race toward the accident. Over months, this narrowed her world. She no longer moved through the city with the easy independence she had before, and the strain of arranging life around rides and refusals began to show in her marriage and at work.

By the time she came for help, Aisha was exhausted by the effort of both thinking about the event and fighting not to think about it. The immediate reason was a recent day at the office when she saw a visitor in the lobby who resembled the injured person closely enough that she had to lock herself in a restroom stall until she could stop shaking. She told herself afterward that she could not keep organizing her life around avoiding cars, commuters, and certain faces, especially when her job required her to be present and collaborative. What frightened her most was the idea that this was now permanent—that one mistake had defined her and that ordinary places like work or the street outside it would never again feel ordinary. What she hoped for, though she said it carefully, was not to erase what happened, but to be able to live alongside the fact of it without feeling ambushed every day by where she works, how she travels, and who she might see.
